input.essay:
Homework and community projects are both important for students and schools should think about how to use them. In the column, Ines Varlow talks about the creek trail in Pell Hollow where eighth graders fix up a trail instead of doing worksheets. Parents are upset because they dont know if their kids can still do math, and the superintendent says the kids learn things from the project that a worksheet can't measure.

I think that community projects are a good thing because students learn by doing. When students are out in the community they learn teamwork and responsibility and how to talk to adults. Varlow says the students had to persuade a town council to fund a footbridge, which is a real life skill. Projects also help the community which is good for everyone. Students will remember a project for a long time but they forget worksheets.

On the other hand homework is important too. Homework is practice and you need practice to get good at something. For example in math you have to do problems over and over or you will not remember how to do them. If kids do not do homework they might fall behind and then they will have trouble on tests. So parents have a point when they worry about the polynomials.

In conclusion, both sides are half right like Varlow says. Schools should use community projects but not get rid of homework completely, and they should find a balance that works for the students. That way students get both the fluency and the experience and everyone is happy.

annotations.quote: Homework and community projects are both important for students and schools should think about how to use them.
annotations.comment: This only says schools should think about both. It restates the prompt and takes no position on how far replacement should go, so it earns no thesis point.

annotations.quote: Schools should use community projects but not get rid of homework completely, and they should find a balance that works for the students.
annotations.comment: Gestures at a middle position, but 'a balance' is vague and obvious. It never says what ratio, in which subjects, or who decides.

annotations.quote: Varlow says the students had to persuade a town council to fund a footbridge, which is a real life skill.
annotations.comment: The evidence comes straight from the column and is only summarized. The commentary just labels it a 'real life skill' and does not connect it to how much homework a project can replace.

annotations.quote: Students will remember a project for a long time but they forget worksheets.
annotations.comment: A general claim with no specific example from the writer's own experience or observation. The essay reads as a list of opinions.

annotations.quote: For example in math you have to do problems over and over or you will not remember how to do them.
annotations.comment: This is the closest the essay comes to a specific example, but it stays general. It does not explain why a project could not build that skill, so it does not address the question of extent.

annotations.quote: both sides are half right like Varlow says
annotations.comment: This borrows the column's own framing. The essay treats homework and projects as simply good and never distinguishes kinds of homework or projects, or notices the question of who sets the ratio, so it earns no sophistication.

input.essay:
On my grandmother's street there is a set of forty-one concrete steps that runs down from Linden Avenue to the bus stop on Carver. I know it's forty-one because I counted them once while carrying her groceries, and also because step twenty-six has been cracked in half for as long as I can remember. The people on Linden shovel those steps after almost every snow. Nobody has ever fixed step twenty-six. To me that staircase answers Marchbank's question better than any of her three camps. Residents should do the light, everyday work that keeps a public step usable, like sweeping, shoveling, and salting. But that duty is only fair if the city keeps the structure itself safe, and it should fall mostly on the people who own property along the steps, not on every resident equally.

First, why should neighbors owe anything at all? Because they're the ones who are there. When it snowed eight inches last January, the city plows cleared Carver by noon, but they don't plow stairs. If Mr. Dunleavy at the top hadn't been out with his shovel at seven, the nurses and kids who take the 6 bus would have been sliding down ice. Shoveling takes twenty minutes and needs no permit and no engineer. A city crew would have to be scheduled and paid and sent across town, and by the time they showed up the snow would have turned into a sheet of ice. For small jobs like this, the person closest to the problem can fix it the fastest, and that's a pretty good reason to make it their job.

Step twenty-six shows where that reasoning stops working, though. You can't shovel your way out of broken concrete, and the neighbors' shoveling actually hides the problem. Since the steps always look cared for, nobody files a complaint, and the city never puts them on a repair list. This is the danger of the "it's your block, it's your shovel" argument. The more neighbors do, the less the city feels it has to do, until the residents are basically holding up infrastructure they don't own. So my position comes with a condition. Neighbors keep the steps passable, the city keeps them standing, and if the city stops doing its part, neighbors shouldn't be expected to just keep sweeping around the crack.

The strongest objection is the one Marchbank mentions about the elderly, renters, and people working two jobs. It's a real problem. My grandmother is eighty-three, and expecting her to shovel forty-one steps would be dangerous and also unfair. The family renting the triplex might be gone by next winter, so they have little reason to invest in a block they won't stay on. That's why I don't think the duty should belong to "residents" in general. It should belong to owners. Homeowners and landlords are the ones whose property values go up when a neighborhood is walkable, so they benefit the most from the steps being kept up. A landlord can hire someone or write shoveling into a lease. Renters and older neighbors can pitch in if they want to, but a rule that fines them for not shoveling would punish the people with the least time and money for something everybody uses.

Underneath all of this is the question of what a public step even is. If it belongs to everyone in an abstract way, it ends up belonging to nobody, which is how step twenty-six stays broken. But if it belongs completely to the people next to it, it starts to feel like their private property, and that isn't right either, since the woman from three streets over walking to the bus has just as much right to it. I think a public step works more like a library book. The city buys it and repairs it, and the people using it every day are expected to keep it in good shape. Neither one can do the other's job, and the staircase on Linden is what happens when only one side does its part.

annotations.quote: Residents should do the light, everyday work that keeps a public step usable, like sweeping, shoveling, and salting.
annotations.comment: Commits to a clear, disputable claim and names the kinds of maintenance residents owe instead of saying 'it depends.' This earns the thesis point.

annotations.quote: But that duty is only fair if the city keeps the structure itself safe, and it should fall mostly on the people who own property along the steps
annotations.comment: Adds two conditions (the city has to keep the structure safe, and owners bear more of the duty than other residents) that set up the essay's line of reasoning: why neighbors owe anything, where that stops, and who exactly owes it.

annotations.quote: If Mr. Dunleavy at the top hadn't been out with his shovel at seven
annotations.comment: A specific observed example, and the writer explains it instead of just dropping it in: comparing the plow schedule with one neighbor's twenty minutes supports the claim that the person closest to the problem can fix small jobs fastest.

annotations.quote: Since the steps always look cared for, nobody files a complaint, and the city never puts them on a repair list.
annotations.comment: The evidence builds on the previous paragraph. The same staircase is used to show the limit of the first point, and that limit is what justifies the city-first condition in the thesis.

annotations.quote: That's why I don't think the duty should belong to "residents" in general. It should belong to owners.
annotations.comment: Takes on the strongest competing view (burdening the elderly and renters) using concrete cases, then adjusts the position instead of brushing the objection aside. This is what the top of the row asks for.

annotations.quote: Homeowners and landlords are the ones whose property values go up when a neighborhood is walkable
annotations.comment: Supports the owner-based duty with an argument about who benefits, so the change to the position is reasoned rather than just asserted.

annotations.quote: The more neighbors do, the less the city feels it has to do
annotations.comment: Points out a tension inside the writer's own position: volunteer upkeep can make it easier for the city to quietly stop investing. This idea is built into the argument and actually shapes the thesis.

annotations.quote: If it belongs to everyone in an abstract way, it ends up belonging to nobody
annotations.comment: Places the issue in a broader question of what public space is for, and works through both extremes, so the nuance is argued out rather than tacked on at the end.

annotations.quote: I think a public step works more like a library book.
annotations.comment: The analogy sums up how responsibility is divided between the city and the users. Together with the step twenty-six thread that runs through the essay, it shows controlled, purposeful style and keeps the complexity going across the whole essay.

In her talk to the Harrow Bend tech crew, Marisol Quade uses personal experience, a story, and a metaphor to change how the students think about being unseen, so that what feels like a loss becomes something to be proud of. Her audience is tired and discouraged, so she has to do more than just tell them their work matters.

Quade starts by building her credibility. She says "Thirty-one years ago I stood where you are standing, holding a roll of glow tape," which tells the students she was once in their position and was a crew member too. This matters because teenagers who feel overlooked might not listen to someone who has never felt that way. Then she lists the things the audience will not see, like the cable and the sandbag, and ends with the single word "Good." The word is short compared to the long sentence before it, and it surprises the crew because it makes not being noticed sound like the goal. She also asks questions like "Why spend six weeks building a world for other people to stand in?" These questions say out loud what the students have been complaining about, so they know she is listening to them.

The biggest part of her argument is the story of Theodora Vance. Theodora saved the show by dropping the sky in early when the actor missed his cue, but the review praised the actor instead. Quade says Theodora "laughed until the driver asked if she was all right." This example shows the crew that someone who was not credited could still be happy about it. It also proves that crew work can be very important, since the audience gasped at the weather. Quade then follows up with the metaphor that the crew is "the circulatory system" and the actors are the face while "you are the pulse." This comparison shows that something can be necessary even if nobody admires it. She also lists what the crew did this month, such as "two hundred and six lighting cues," which gives them specific proof of their work.

Quade also admits that it is not fair. She says "I would be lying if I told you it never stung" and tells about the night in Lissenbrook when the booth was skipped at the cast party. By admitting this she seems honest, so the students are more likely to believe her when she says "Invisibility is the proof that you did it right." She does not just give a pep talk, she shows she has felt what they feel.

At the end the tone changes and she gives commands, "listen," "Thank each other," and "check your headset." The ending is practical and not dramatic, which fits the crew's job of doing small things well. Overall, Quade gets the students ready for opening night by showing them their invisible work is a kind of success.

annotations.quote: uses personal experience, a story, and a metaphor to change how the students think about being unseen, so that what feels like a loss becomes something to be proud of
annotations.comment: Defensible claim about how Quade's choices work on this audience (reframing invisibility from loss to achievement). It names choices and a function, so it earns the thesis point.

annotations.quote: which tells the students she was once in their position and was a crew member too
annotations.comment: Correctly identifies the opening ethos appeal and ties it to the audience, but the commentary is fairly general and mostly restates what the quotation says.

annotations.quote: The word is short compared to the long sentence before it, and it surprises the crew because it makes not being noticed sound like the goal.
annotations.comment: Accurately notes the ironic 'Good' and sentence-length contrast and links it to the crew's complaint. This is one of the stronger, more specific moments.

annotations.quote: These questions say out loud what the students have been complaining about, so they know she is listening to them.
annotations.comment: Connects the rhetorical questions to the crew's situation, but the explanation stays brief and does not show how the questions set up the answers that follow.

annotations.quote: This example shows the crew that someone who was not credited could still be happy about it.
annotations.comment: Explains the Theodora anecdote's purpose for the crew, though it largely summarizes the story and does not discuss the ironic review in depth.

annotations.quote: This comparison shows that something can be necessary even if nobody admires it.
annotations.comment: Names the metaphor and gives a general effect; the commentary is repetitive and does not examine the face/pulse antithesis or why a body image suits these students.

annotations.quote: By admitting this she seems honest, so the students are more likely to believe her
annotations.comment: Good point that the concession earns trust, but it is treated as one item in a list and not linked back to the earlier moves to build a line of reasoning.

annotations.quote: The ending is practical and not dramatic, which fits the crew's job of doing small things well.
annotations.comment: Touches on the understated ending, but the observation is brief and not developed into a sustained insight about how the argument accumulates or about the tension between reward and sting, so sophistication is not earned.

In her Landing Day speech, Ines Marrow tries to change how Birch Landing sees the delays she caused by turning the town's complaints into proof that she cared about them. She does this mostly through numbers, a personal story, and a personified river, which together make waiting look like a skill instead of fear.

Marrow starts by using numbers to build her credibility. She says she made "something close to forty thousand crossings" but also refused "about six hundred." Putting the two numbers next to each other shows the audience that refusals were rare, so they were not a habit of a nervous captain. This matters for commuters who are used to being annoyed with her, because it suggests that the delays were a small part of her work. She also describes the fog "like a lid on a pot," which is a homey comparison that people in a river town would understand. Then she uses a colon before the word "wait," which makes the word stand out as the thing nobody wants to hear. This shows she understands how the audience feels, and that makes them more willing to listen to her.

The strongest part of her argument is the story about Dell Ambrose. His wife was in labor, and he told her he would never forgive her, but she "kept it tied." The short sentence "I kept it tied" sounds firm and shows she did not give in even under huge pressure. The story has a happy ending, since the fog lifted and the baby was born safely, so the audience sees that waiting worked. Marrow also says "I do not tell that story to make myself the hero of it," which makes her seem modest. This emotional story makes the audience feel that the delay was worth it, and it proves her point better than just stating it.

Marrow also admits that "patience can be a disguise for timidity." By conceding this, she seems honest and fair instead of defensive. Then she says that a captain who waits too long is better than one who leaves early, because only one has to "stand up in a church and explain herself." This makes the audience think about the worst outcome, and it makes their complaints seem small. The river is described as something that "does not negotiate," which shows that the delays were not her choice but the river's, so she cannot be blamed.

At the end her tone gets softer. She says "You forgave me, mostly," which is a little funny and shows she knows the town was angry. She finishes with the idea that "silence is sometimes the sound of somebody taking care of you." This ties the whole speech together by making the quiet horn into a sign of care. It also speaks to the new captain and tells the town to be patient with whoever comes next.

Overall, Marrow uses statistics, a story, and a gentle ending to persuade the town that waiting is care. Each choice makes the audience see her refusals differently, so by the end they thank her for the crossings they did not make.

annotations.quote: turning the town's complaints into proof that she cared about them
annotations.comment: Defensible thesis that claims how Marrow reframes the grievance as care and names strategies (numbers, story, personified river). Earns the thesis point even though the preview is somewhat list-like.

annotations.quote: Putting the two numbers next to each other shows the audience that refusals were rare, so they were not a habit of a nervous captain.
annotations.comment: Accurately explains the contrast of 40,000 and 600 and links it to the charge of timidity. Good commentary, but it stays fairly general about how it works on commuters.

annotations.quote: Then she uses a colon before the word "wait," which makes the word stand out as the thing nobody wants to hear.
annotations.comment: Identifies the colon and isolated word with a brief effect, but the follow-up claim that this makes people 'more willing to listen' is generic.

annotations.quote: which makes her seem modest
annotations.comment: Notices the disclaimer of hero status but treats it only as modesty. Does not see the tension that she is plainly right in the story, so the anecdote commentary stays at emotional effect and is limited.

annotations.quote: This emotional story makes the audience feel that the delay was worth it
annotations.comment: Commentary is general and leans on 'emotional'; it does not explain how the story turns into an argument about judgment.

annotations.quote: so she cannot be blamed
annotations.comment: Brief and slightly off: the personified river is used to say the captain's only power is to match its hours, not to excuse herself. Thin explanation of the choice.

annotations.quote: It also speaks to the new captain and tells the town to be patient with whoever comes next.
annotations.comment: Gestures at the occasion and successor, but only in one sentence and not developed, so it does not earn sophistication.

annotations.quote: Each choice makes the audience see her refusals differently, so by the end they thank her for the crossings they did not make.
annotations.comment: Conclusion mostly repeats the thesis and misattributes the thanks to the audience; it does not explain how the accusers become co-owners of the safe record.

Fruit and nut trees on public land is a topic that has a lot of different sides to it. Some people like it and some people dont, and the sources show both. In my opinion cities should think carefully about planting fruit trees, because there are good things and bad things about it.

Source A is about Marlow Bend which planted plums and other trees on Orchard Boulevard. The article says there were 212 service requests last year about fallen plums and wasps. It also says that the Boulevard Gleaners gave 2,300 pounds of fruit to pantries. So this shows that there are problems but also benefits to the trees. The superintendent says trees with a block captain look great.

Source B is a column by Corwin Ashby-Feld who does not like the idea. He says a plum tree fruits for three weeks but hunger lasts fifty-two. He also says the fruit goes to whoever has a ladder. He thinks cities should plant shade and give money to the food bank instead. This is a strong argument against the trees.

Source D is a personal essay about a serviceberry tree at the library. The writer met Mr. Haldane there and her daughter ate the berries. She says the tree gives people a reason to talk to each other. This shows a good side of the trees that is not about food.

Source E has a survey where 68 percent agree with parks but only 41 percent agree with streets. This shows people like parks more.

In conclusion, there are pros and cons to fruit trees on public land. Cities should look at both sides before they decide, and the sources help show what to think about.

annotations.quote: Fruit and nut trees on public land is a topic that has a lot of different sides to it.
annotations.comment: Only announces the topic and says there are many sides; no position a reader could disagree with.

annotations.quote: cities should think carefully about planting fruit trees, because there are good things and bad things about it.
annotations.comment: Does not commit to a position or name a condition; this is the 'pros and cons' thesis that earns no credit.

annotations.quote: It also says that the Boulevard Gleaners gave 2,300 pounds of fruit to pantries.
annotations.comment: Accurate specific detail from Source A, but it is summary; the essay never explains what it proves for an argument.

annotations.quote: This is a strong argument against the trees.
annotations.comment: Commentary is a vague judgment that does not engage Source B's claims or answer them with other sources.

annotations.quote: Source E has a survey where 68 percent agree with parks but only 41 percent agree with streets.
annotations.comment: Cites real numbers but only restates them. The essay never connects them to the Source A or F cost data or to a claim about where to plant.

annotations.quote: Source B is a column by Corwin Ashby-Feld who does not like the idea.
annotations.comment: Paragraphs are organized source by source rather than around the writer's own claims, so the sources are listed, not put in conversation.

annotations.quote: In conclusion, there are pros and cons to fruit trees on public land.
annotations.comment: Stays at a generic pro-versus-con level with no weighing of source reliability or broader context, so no sophistication is shown.

Libraries lending tools is a topic with a lot of different opinions. Some people think it is a good idea and some people think it is a bad idea. In this essay I will look at both sides and talk about what the sources say.

Source A says that libraries should lend drills because the mission of a library is access and not paper. The writer's neighbor needed a drill for forty minutes and he got one for free. Source A also says sewing machines went out 2,300 times. This shows that people like borrowing things from the library.

On the other hand Source B says that the library should not expand its tools. It says the non-book collection used 3.8 percent of the budget and only 3.1 percent of circulation. It also says staff spent 140 hours on maintenance. So there are problems with cost and staff time and liability too because a patron cut his hand on a jigsaw.

Source D is from a man who owns a rental shop and he thinks the library should leave the tools to people who know them. He says he would be funding a competitor with his taxes. He has some good points but he also might just want to protect his business.

Source C is an interview with a library director who says it worked in Marrowfield. Objects are 2 percent of the budget and over 4 percent of checkouts. But she also says there are waiting lists and some things were stolen.

In conclusion there are good things and bad things about libraries lending tools. Libraries should think about it carefully before they decide. It depends on the library and the town.

annotations.quote: Source A says that libraries should lend drills because the mission of a library is access and not paper.

annotations.quote: This shows that people like borrowing things from the library.
annotations.comment: A vague generalization drawn from the 2,300 figure. It does not interpret what the number does or does not show, for example by comparing it with Source E's upkeep costs.

annotations.comment: Reports the Source B figures without noticing that they match Castlebrook in Source F, or that Castlebrook is an outlier against Marrowfield's 2.1 versus 4.3. No integration of sources and no interpretation.

annotations.quote: He has some good points but he also might just want to protect his business.

annotations.quote: In conclusion there are good things and bad things about libraries lending tools.

I think residents should be responsible for the everyday upkeep of the sidewalks and steps near their homes, like sweeping, shoveling, and clearing leaves, but the city should always pay for real repairs like broken concrete or steps that are falling apart. The line should be drawn between things a regular person can do with a broom and things that need a contractor.

My grandmother lives on a street in our town with a long set of stone steps that connects her road to the one below it. Every fall the steps get covered in wet leaves and in winter they ice over. The neighbors on both sides take turns clearing them, and a few of them put down salt. This works because it is easy and it does not cost much. Everybody who lives there uses the steps, so everybody has a reason to keep them safe. If one neighbor did not help, it would still be only a small amount of work for the others. This shows that routine upkeep is something a neighborhood can reasonably share, since the people who use a sidewalk the most are the ones who notice when it is dangerous.

However, the same steps have a cracked section near the bottom that has been there for years. My grandmother called the city about it twice. Nobody expected the neighbors to fix it, and they shouldn't have to. Fixing concrete costs real money and takes tools and training, and if someone fixed it badly and a person got hurt, the neighbors might be blamed. That is why the city should handle structural repairs. The city already collects taxes, and it owns the steps, so it should be the one to keep them from falling apart.

Some people would say that even sweeping and shoveling is too much to ask, because of people like my grandmother who is in her seventies and cannot shovel anymore. This is a good point and I do not think the rule should be the same for everyone. Younger neighbors can help the elderly ones, and people who cannot do it should not be punished or fined. Renters who work long hours might also have trouble finding time. So the responsibility should be shared by the whole block instead of put on each person alone, and the city should step in when a block really cannot manage.

In conclusion, neighbors should keep the steps passable because they are the ones who use them every day, but the city has to be responsible for anything that is broken. If both do their part, the steps will not be nobody's child anymore.

annotations.quote: residents should be responsible for the everyday upkeep of the sidewalks and steps near their homes, like sweeping, shoveling, and clearing leaves, but the city should always pay for real repairs
annotations.comment: Clear, defensible qualified thesis that draws a real line between routine upkeep and structural repair, so it earns the thesis point.

annotations.quote: My grandmother lives on a street in our town with a long set of stone steps that connects her road to the one below it.
annotations.comment: Specific personal observation, but much of this paragraph is description of the scene rather than analysis, so the evidence is partly summary.

annotations.quote: This shows that routine upkeep is something a neighborhood can reasonably share, since the people who use a sidewalk the most are the ones who notice when it is dangerous.
annotations.comment: Commentary does link the example to the claim, but it is fairly general and repeats the thesis rather than building a deeper line of reasoning.

annotations.quote: Fixing concrete costs real money and takes tools and training, and if someone fixed it badly and a person got hurt, the neighbors might be blamed.
annotations.comment: Gives a reason (cost, skill, liability) for the repair half of the thesis, but it is asserted rather than supported with a concrete case.

annotations.quote: So the responsibility should be shared by the whole block instead of put on each person alone, and the city should step in when a block really cannot manage.
annotations.comment: Addresses the elderly and renter objection and adjusts the position, but the treatment is brief and does not explore tensions such as the city using volunteer work to disinvest, so no sustained sophistication.

annotations.quote: If both do their part, the steps will not be nobody's child anymore.
annotations.comment: Conclusion mostly restates the thesis and borrows the stimulus title instead of adding new reasoning.

Public libraries should lend tools and other practical objects, but only when they can fund it separately and stick mostly to items that are cheap to keep up. Libraries have always been about giving people access to things they could not afford alone, and a drill fits that idea as well as a book does, but a library that takes on too much will end up hurting itself.

The strongest reason to lend objects is access. In Source A, Vasquez-Pryor describes a neighbor who could not afford a drill for a forty minute job and borrowed one from the Marrowfield library instead. She argues that the mission of the library was never paper, it was access. I agree with this because a family that saves money on a one-time repair is being served just like a student who borrows a textbook. Source C backs this up from the library's side. Director Brenner says a third of new library cards went to adults who came in for a drill or a sewing machine, and some of them now borrow books too. So lending objects may actually bring people toward the library's core purpose instead of away from it, which answers the critics who say the mission gets diluted.

However, the critics have real points. Source B, the Castlebrook trustees memo, says the non-book collection took 3.8 percent of the budget but only 3.1 percent of circulation, and that staff spent 140 hours on maintenance. Source F shows that Castlebrook is the only library of the five where the budget bar is taller than the circulation bar. At Marrowfield, for example, objects are 2.1 percent of the budget and 4.3 percent of circulation. This suggests that lending can work well, but it does not work automatically. Castlebrook has two part-time clerks and one storage closet, and Brenner admits that a library like that might be better off saying no. I think this means the budget objection is true for some libraries but is not a reason for all libraries to refuse.

The table in Source E shows what kind of items libraries should choose. Cake pans cost only 6 dollars a year in upkeep per item and energy meters cost 9, while instruments cost 57 and sewing machines 44. Brenner says the same thing, to choose items by upkeep and not excitement. Therefore a small library could start with the cheap items and leave the expensive ones for later.

Gunnar Halvorsen in Source D argues that tools should be left to people who know them, because untrained clerks cannot warn people about a tile saw and the shop owner pays taxes that support the library. This is a fair worry about safety, and it is one reason I would not have a small library lend dangerous power equipment like saws. But his own letter admits the library could lend the small things like cake pans and meters, which is exactly what my position says.

In conclusion, libraries should lend practical objects, but with grants, trained staff and low-upkeep items, so that access grows without wrecking the budget.

annotations.quote: In conclusion, libraries should lend practical objects, but with grants, trained staff and low-upkeep items, so that access grows without wrecking the budget.
annotations.comment: Conclusion mostly repeats the thesis and adds no new insight, so there is no sustained sophistication.

Cities should plant fruit and nut trees on public land, but only in parks and school grounds where a volunteer group has agreed to take care of them. Planting them along sidewalks or without anyone in charge causes more problems than it solves.

The biggest reason is cost and mess. In Source A, Marlow Bend replaced its ash trees with edible ones and got 212 service requests in one year, mostly about plums staining sidewalks and attracting wasps. The superintendent says that trees with a block captain look great and the others look like nobody loves them. Source F backs this up with numbers, since a fruit tree with a steward costs 71 dollars a year but one without a steward costs 112, which is more than double the 48 dollars for an ordinary shade tree. This shows that the trees themselves are not the main expense, it is the lack of people looking after them. So if a city plants fruit trees with no plan for who cares for them, it ends up paying a lot more.

Source C makes the same point from a different city. Palumbo's pears downtown were planted because of a grant and nobody asked for them, so they became the ugliest trees he has. The Thistle Park grove, which a seniors' club asked for and signed an agreement about, became the best. His rule of "no steward, no tree" fits my position well. It also answers part of what Source B complains about. Ashby-Feld says the fruit goes to whoever has a ladder and a free Saturday, but Palumbo says Thistle Park has loaner poles and a chalkboard of picking dates, so organization can fix the fairness problem.

However, I have to admit Source B has a point that is harder to answer. A plum tree fruits for three weeks and hunger lasts all year, so public orchards are not a real food policy. Source E also gives a warning, because only 23 percent of residents picked any public fruit and only 29 percent would volunteer. That means finding stewards might be hard, and the steward rule could mean few trees get planted. But I think that is actually fine, since the survey also shows 68 percent support trees in parks while only 41 percent support them on streets. People seem to already understand that parks are the better place.

Source D shows what the trees can give besides food. Marrow met Mr. Haldane because of a serviceberry by the library, something that she says a city cannot measure. This is a personal essay so it is not hard evidence, but it shows why a small number of well-run trees is worth it even if they do not feed the city.

In conclusion, cities should plant edible trees, but in parks, schools and libraries, with a steward group that signs on first.

input.essay:
Schools should replace some homework with long-term community projects, but only in subjects like science and social studies where the project actually uses what students are learning. In math and writing, where skills depend on repeated practice, projects should not take over the nightly work.

Ines Varlow says homework is "practice" and a community project is "something else," and I think that is true. Practice is what makes a skill reliable. When I was in Algebra I, I did not really understand factoring until I did about twenty problems in a row one night and finally saw the pattern. A community project could not have given me that, because a project does not repeat the same step enough times. If the Pell Hollow students spend the whole spring on the creek trail, some of them might forget how to factor a polynomial, which is what the parents were worried about. So in math I think homework has to stay, because the fluency comes from the repetition.

On the other hand, there are subjects where a project teaches more than a worksheet. My cousin's school in another town had an environmental science class that tested the water in a local pond every month for a year. They had to collect samples, record numbers, and write a report for the town. He learned how to use a graph because he needed one, and he remembered the data much better than he remembered any worksheet. This shows that when the project requires the same skill the class is teaching, it can replace the homework, since the students are practicing anyway but with a real purpose. The superintendent in the column is right that persuading a town council teaches something a worksheet does not, but that is mostly a speaking and civics skill, so it fits best in a social studies class.

Some people would say projects are unfair because not every student has a ride or free afternoons. That is a real problem. A student who works after school or lives far from the site cannot put in forty hours the way another student can. For this reason schools should give class time for the project and not make it all extra work at home. If they cannot do that, then the project should be a smaller part of the grade.

In the end, the extent of replacement should depend on the subject and not be one rule for the whole district. Varlow asks who should set the ratio, and I think teachers should, since they know whether the project and the skill match. Projects can replace part of homework, but not all of it, and not in every class.

annotations.quote: Schools should replace some homework with long-term community projects, but only in subjects like science and social studies where the project actually uses what students are learning.
annotations.comment: Clear, defensible thesis that takes a position on extent (some replacement, limited by subject and skill match), not just whether projects are good. Earns the thesis point.

annotations.quote: I did not really understand factoring until I did about twenty problems in a row one night and finally saw the pattern.
annotations.comment: Specific personal evidence that a reader can picture, and it is tied to the claim that math needs repetition. Commentary is brief, though, so it is only partly developed.

annotations.quote: My cousin's school in another town had an environmental science class that tested the water in a local pond every month for a year.
annotations.comment: Concrete observed example of a project replacing practice. The follow-up explains the link (a real purpose for graphing), but the reasoning stays fairly general and slightly repeats the first body paragraph's point.

annotations.quote: That is a real problem.
annotations.comment: The equity objection is raised and given a modest fix (class time), but it is handled quickly with no specific example, so engagement with the counterargument is thin.

annotations.quote: Varlow asks who should set the ratio, and I think teachers should, since they know whether the project and the skill match.
annotations.comment: Notices the column's question about who decides, but only in a single closing sentence without developing it, so the argument stays flat and no sophistication point is earned.

In her speech to the stage crew Marisol Quade uses many rhetorical choices to convince them that their work is important even though the audience does not see it. She uses stories, metaphors, and a lot of details to make her point and it is very effective for the crew.

Quade starts out by telling the crew she was in their position thirty-one years ago. This shows she has experience so the students will listen to her. She says "Tomorrow night four hundred people will fill those seats, and not one of them will know your names." Then she says "Good." This is a short sentence after long ones and it surprises the reader. It shows that not being seen is a good thing.

Next she tells a story about a girl named Theodora Vance who ran the fly rail. Theodora saved the show by dropping the sky early but the review praised the actor instead. This story is used to show the crew that people do not notice the work but it still matters. Theodora laughed about it, which shows she was proud anyway. The story makes the point more real than just saying it.

Quade also uses a metaphor and compares the crew to a circulatory system. She says "The actors are the face; you are the pulse." This makes the crew feel important because without a pulse the body dies. She also lists what they did like "eleven set pieces, two hundred and six lighting cues" so they can see how much they did.

At the end she says to thank each other and check your headset. This tells them what to do and it ends the speech. Overall Quade uses these choices to make the tired crew feel better about their work and ready for opening night.

annotations.quote: Marisol Quade uses many rhetorical choices to convince them that their work is important even though the audience does not see it.
annotations.comment: Mostly restates the prompt. It names no specific claim about how her choices reframe invisibility for a tired crew, so it does not earn the thesis point.

annotations.quote: This shows she has experience so the students will listen to her.
annotations.comment: Identifies the ethos appeal but only labels it. It does not explain why a veteran's shared history matters to discouraged teenagers.

annotations.quote: This is a short sentence after long ones and it surprises the reader.
annotations.comment: Correctly notices the sentence-length contrast and the ironic 'Good'. However, it speaks of 'the reader' and not the crew, and the effect is only partly explained.

annotations.quote: The story makes the point more real than just saying it.
annotations.comment: General commentary. It does not discuss the irony of the review praising the actor or how that answers the crew's complaint about going unnoticed.

annotations.quote: This makes the crew feel important because without a pulse the body dies.
annotations.comment: Some real explanation of the metaphor tied to the audience. It is brief and not connected to the other choices.

annotations.quote: Overall Quade uses these choices to make the tired crew feel better about their work and ready for opening night.
annotations.comment: The conclusion repeats the earlier points. The essay treats the choices as a list. It skips the concession about the stinging unfairness and does not trace how the talk builds, so there is no sophistication.

Sidewalks and steps are a big part of any neighborhood and everybody uses them. The question of who should take care of them is a hard one because there are good points on both sides. In my opinion the residents and the city both have a responsibility to keep the sidewalks and steps in good shape.

On one hand, residents live right next to the sidewalks so they should help. If you live on a street you see the sidewalk every day and you walk on it, so it makes sense that you would want it to be clean. My grandmother lives on a hill and there are steps near her house that get covered in leaves every fall. Some of her neighbors rake them but some do not. This shows that when people do not help, things get messy and that is not good for the neighborhood.

On the other hand, the city is supposed to take care of public property because people pay taxes. Taxes are for things like roads and sidewalks. If the city does not do its job then taxes are being wasted. Also some people are old or work a lot so they cannot always help out. It would not be fair to make them do it.

In conclusion, there are many reasons why both the residents and the city should share the work. Everyone benefits from nice sidewalks so everyone should do their part. If everybody works together the town will be a better place to live and the sidewalks and steps will be safe for everyone.

annotations.quote: In my opinion the residents and the city both have a responsibility to keep the sidewalks and steps in good shape.
annotations.comment: This thesis only says both sides share responsibility, which restates the prompt and draws no line between routine upkeep and structural repair. It does not commit to a claim a reader could dispute, so it earns no thesis credit.

annotations.quote: My grandmother lives on a hill and there are steps near her house that get covered in leaves every fall.
annotations.comment: This is the one specific example, but it is thin. The commentary ('things get messy and that is not good') just asserts a point and never ties the example to how much responsibility residents should bear.

annotations.quote: Taxes are for things like roads and sidewalks. If the city does not do its job then taxes are being wasted.
annotations.comment: This is a general statement with no concrete evidence. It repeats one of the camps from the stimulus without developing it or answering it.

annotations.quote: Some people are old or work a lot so they cannot always help out. It would not be fair to make them do it.
annotations.comment: It mentions the burden on the elderly and on people working long hours, but only in passing. It never reconciles this with the earlier claim that residents should help, so the essay contradicts itself instead of building an argument.

annotations.quote: Everyone benefits from nice sidewalks so everyone should do their part.
annotations.comment: The essay treats the question as simple agreement with both sides and repeats one idea. It never separates kinds of maintenance or kinds of residents and never explores the limits of its position, so it earns no sophistication credit.

When most people picture a library they picture shelves of books, so a library that lends a pressure washer sounds a little strange. But the real question isn't whether a drill belongs next to a novel. It's whether a town can share things no single household can justify buying, and whether the library has the money and staff to do the sharing well. Public libraries should lend practical objects, but they should start with cheap, sturdy items like cake pans and energy meters, and they should add power tools and other high-upkeep equipment only when outside funding covers repairs. Lending without that money doesn't extend the library's mission. It eats into it.

Vasquez-Pryor (Source A) argues that "the mission was never paper," it was access, and the best evidence that she is right comes from Source C, not her own column. Brenner reports that about a third of Marrowfield's new library cards went to adults who came in for a drill or sewing machine, and "some of them now borrow books." That flips the critics' worry about dilution. If objects bring back adults who haven't had a card since childhood, the tool shelf is feeding the book shelf, not competing with it. This is also something a circulation count can't show, since a loan is counted the same whether it is someone's hundredth checkout or the reason they came back at all.

The budget objection in Source B is serious, but it says more about Castlebrook than about tool lending. The board writes that objects took 3.8 percent of its budget and produced only 3.1 percent of circulation, and Source F shows these exact numbers. In the chart, though, Castlebrook is the only one of five libraries where the budget bar is taller than the circulation bar. Marrowfield spends 2.1 percent for 4.3 percent of circulation, and Reedham spends 2.6 for 6.0. So the problem is not objects themselves but how Castlebrook pays for them. Its own memo admits it has "no dedicated funding" and "one storage closet," while Brenner started with a foundation grant and has a credit union paying for repairs. Even the board's last line, "fund one directly," basically agrees with Brenner. They only disagree about where the collection should be housed. I should admit that five libraries from one cooperative is a small sample, and a cooperative that publishes a newsletter cheering on tool lending may not be neutral, but the pattern still points to funding as the deciding factor.

Source E shows which objects to start with. Cake pans cost about $6 a year in upkeep and energy meters $9, compared to $44 for sewing machines and $57 for instruments. The cheap items aren't unpopular either: cake pans had 4,120 loans, almost twice the 2,300 for sewing machines (the same figure Source A brags about). The table gives total loans, not loans per item, so it can't prove which category costs least per checkout. Still, it does show that 27 libraries lend meters and only 11 lend instruments, which suggests libraries are already sorting items by upkeep, just as Brenner advises.

Halvorsen (Source D) makes the strongest case against me. A clerk running story hour can't check a tile saw's fence, and Source B's jigsaw injury shows the risk is real. But look at what he proposes: the library should lend "the cake pans and the meters." That is the same line I draw. Where I disagree is his voucher plan for everything else. Vasquez-Pryor's neighbor needed a drill for forty minutes, and paperwork plus a trip to a rental shop is exactly the kind of barrier a library removes. His idea of a community college safety class fits the dangerous tools, like tile saws, but not a basic drill.

The seven-week waiting list for a sewing machine in Source C is the best warning for both sides. People do need these objects, and a library that offers them without money to meet the demand ends up failing "exactly the people we meant to serve." Libraries should lend things, but only as many things as they can afford to take care of.

Every city has trees that nobody really owns. They belong to "the public," which in practice means whichever parks crew gets the phone calls. Fruit trees make that problem obvious, because a plum tree nobody cares for doesn't just stand there. It drops its fruit on somebody's shoe. Cities should plant fruit and nut trees on public land, but only in parks, schoolyards and library lawns, and only where a group of residents has signed on to care for the trees and share the harvest before the tree goes in. The tree is the easy part. The people are the actual program.

The strongest evidence for this is the stewardship numbers. In Marlow Bend, a fruit tree with a volunteer steward costs the city $71 a year, and one with no steward costs $112 (Source A, Source F). That $41 gap is almost the entire cost of an ordinary shade tree ($48). So an unloved fruit tree costs more than twice as much as a shade tree, but a cared-for one costs only about $23 more. Nut trees show the same pattern, $64 versus $98. Superintendent Threlkeld puts it bluntly: trees without a block captain "look like nobody loves them, because nobody does." Palumbo in Verrin Heights (Source C) learned the same lesson from both directions. His grant-funded sidewalk pears are "the ugliest trees we own," while the grove a seniors' club asked for at Thistle Park became "the best trees we own." His rule, "no steward, no tree," is basically the cost chart turned into a policy.

Location matters almost as much as stewardship. Caddis Falls residents support fruit trees in parks 68 percent to 19, but on residential streets they split 41 to 44 (Source E). That doesn't mean people hate fruit. It means they don't want plums on the sidewalk in front of their own house. Council member Adebanjo-Lind voted for the Marlow Bend program, but he now says "a plum tree over a bus stop was a mistake," which is the same line the survey draws. Palumbo's "polite fruit," like persimmons that hang on until someone picks them, takes care of a lot of the mess complaint too.

Ashby-Feld (Source B) makes the best case against, and he is right about some things. A three-week plum season is not a food policy, and a hungry family needs a pantry that's open in February. But his column is an opinion piece aimed at the weakest version of the idea: a sidewalk plum with no plan behind it. His most serious point is fairness, that the harvest goes to "whoever has a ladder." Palumbo, though, describes the fixes for exactly that: loaner poles for people who can't climb, a chalkboard of picking dates, and a rule that the first basket goes to the Ferrow Street pantry. Ashby-Feld sees the race and decides not to plant. Palumbo sees the same race and decides to organize it. And since the Boulevard Gleaners carried 2,300 pounds of fruit to church pantries, the trees and the food bank don't have to be rivals.

Still, the steward rule has a cost I don't want to skip over. Only 29 percent of Caddis Falls residents say they would volunteer (Source E). The neighborhoods most likely to have a seniors' club with free afternoons may not be the ones that need free fruit the most. Left alone, "no steward, no tree" could put orchards mainly in neighborhoods that are already organized. So cities should help create stewards instead of just waiting for them to show up, for example by pairing a school or library with a local pantry.

This matters because, as Marrow writes in Source D, the fruit is really "the excuse." Her shy daughter and Mr. Haldane only met because of a serviceberry. Her essay is one family's story, and only 23 percent of residents picked anything last year, so I wouldn't build a budget on it. But it explains something the cost chart can't, which is why a city might pay that extra $23. Shade falls on everyone equally, like Ashby-Feld says, but it has never gotten two strangers talking.

annotations.comment: This is a conditional thesis that names both of its conditions, location and a steward who commits before planting. It also sets up the line of reasoning the body paragraphs follow. That earns the point.

annotations.quote: That $41 gap is almost the entire cost of an ordinary shade tree ($48).
annotations.comment: The essay notices that Source A's figures match Source F and then interprets them instead of just listing them. Comparing the gap to the shade-tree cost shows what the numbers mean.

annotations.quote: is basically the cost chart turned into a policy
annotations.comment: This ties Palumbo's qualitative rule to the quantitative data, so the text and data sources are in conversation instead of sitting in separate paragraphs.

annotations.quote: That doesn't mean people hate fruit. It means they don't want plums on the sidewalk in front of their own house.
annotations.comment: The writer explains what the gap between support for parks and support for streets in Source E shows, then connects it to Adebanjo-Lind in Source A to back up the location condition.

annotations.quote: Ashby-Feld sees the race and decides not to plant. Palumbo sees the same race and decides to organize it.
annotations.comment: The writer takes on the counterargument directly. Source C's loaner poles and pantry rule answer Source B's fairness objection, and the line shows the two sources reaching opposite conclusions about the same problem. This is Row B level 4 work.

annotations.quote: Left alone, "no steward, no tree" could put orchards mainly in neighborhoods that are already organized.
annotations.comment: The writer points out a limit of their own position, that it could be unfair about who public goods reach, and proposes a fix. A full paragraph develops this, so it is a sustained move and not a one-line hedge.

annotations.quote: But his column is an opinion piece aimed at the weakest version of the idea
annotations.comment: The essay weighs what kind of source each one is and what it is for. It does this here with the op-ed and again later with the personal essay ('one family's story... I wouldn't build a budget on it'), so the move carries across the essay and supports the Row C point.

annotations.comment: The writer checks Source D's claim against Source E's participation number and limits how much weight the anecdote can carry, while still using it to explain the community value. This is another case of weighing sources by reliability.

The night before opening, after a long dress rehearsal, a tired high school crew does not need to be told their work is glamorous, because they know it isn't. Marisol Quade seems to understand this. Instead of promising the crew recognition they will never get, she redefines invisibility, turning it from an insult into proof that they did the job right. She builds this in stages: she voices the crew's complaints for them, answers those complaints with a story and a metaphor that make unseen work feel essential, and then admits the arrangement hurts, so that her final commands sound like advice from someone who has been there and not like a pep talk.

Quade opens by standing where the students stand. "Thirty-one years ago I stood where you are standing" gives her authority, but it also tells the crew she once felt the same way, "wondering why I had signed up for a job nobody would clap for." Then she lists what they actually did that day: "the forty feet of cable you coiled this afternoon," the sandbag "re-tied twice because the first knot felt wrong." The students' complaint is that nobody notices, and in the first paragraph a speaker shows that she noticed. Then comes the one-word sentence "Good." After a long, heavy list, it is jarring, and I think it's meant to be. The crew expects sympathy and gets a challenge, which makes them want to hear why being unnoticed could possibly be good.

Next she says their doubts out loud. "Why spend six weeks building a world for other people to stand in?" Because she admits "some of you are thinking" this, nobody has to complain, and she gets to answer them directly. Her answer is an antithesis: "the dark is not where the play hides from you; it is where the play depends on you." For a crew, "the dark" means being hidden, and she flips it so it means being trusted.

The Theodora story makes that flip concrete. When the actor jumped his cue, Theodora "did not panic, did not wait for me, did not check the book," and the next day's review praised "the actor's uncanny timing." The irony is obvious, since the credit went to the wrong person, but Theodora laughs instead of resenting it. "That laugh is the whole job," Quade says, meaning the crew gets to know a secret the audience doesn't. The circulatory-system metaphor pushes this further: "The actors are the face; you are the pulse." Students who feel minor are told they are the part a body can't live without. Even her count, "two hundred and six lighting cues," does what the audience won't, which is to add up their work.

What makes the speech convincing, though, is that Quade doesn't pretend this is all fine. "I will admit the arrangement is not fair," she says, and she remembers the night in Lissenbrook when she "drove home with the radio off." If she had only said invisibility is a reward, teenagers who feel cheated would probably hear an adult explaining away something unfair. By admitting it stung, she holds both ideas together. "Invisibility is the proof that you did it right" comes after the hurt, not instead of it, so the crew can believe it without having to pretend they aren't disappointed.

The ending finishes the argument without a big flourish. "No one will ever thank you for it. Thank each other." Since thanks won't come from the audience, she gives the crew a replacement they control. Then: "Then check your headset, and let's go." A speech about work nobody sees ends on a small, practical task instead of a grand line. That understatement suits a speaker who values quiet competence, and it turns the crew's discouragement back toward the job in front of them.

annotations.comment: Defensible thesis about how Quade's approach works toward her purpose, not just a list of devices.

annotations.quote: She builds this in stages
annotations.comment: Sets up a line of reasoning (voicing doubts, answering them, conceding) that the body paragraphs follow in order.

annotations.quote: in the first paragraph a speaker shows that she noticed
annotations.comment: Explains why the specific details matter to students who feel unnoticed, not just that they are 'vivid.'

annotations.quote: The crew expects sympathy and gets a challenge
annotations.comment: Ties the fragment 'Good' and the change in sentence length to how this discouraged audience is likely to react.

annotations.quote: she flips it so it means being trusted
annotations.comment: Accurate commentary on the antithesis in sentence 9 as an answer to the doubts voiced in sentences 6-7, which builds the line of reasoning.

annotations.quote: Students who feel minor are told they are the part a body can't live without
annotations.comment: Connects the face/pulse metaphor to the crew's specific feeling of being minor.

annotations.quote: Even her count, "two hundred and six lighting cues," does what the audience won't
annotations.comment: A brief but purposeful point about the enumeration, linked back to the thesis about recognition.

annotations.quote: would probably hear an adult explaining away something unfair

On her last night as captain, Ines Marrow is speaking to a crowd that has spent thirty-one years waiting on her. Some of the people at Landing Day have missed shifts and school because she would not leave the dock, and she knows it. Instead of defending her record against them, Marrow folds their complaints into her argument. She admits exactly what her refusals cost, concedes that patience can sometimes be cowardice, and finally thanks the town for "the ones we did not make." In doing this she turns her audience's grievance into proof that waiting was care, and she prepares them to give the next captain the trust they only reluctantly gave her.

Marrow starts by showing that she is not a captain who looks for reasons to stay tied up. She tells them she made "something close to forty thousand crossings" and refused "about six hundred." The numbers matter because to a commuter stuck on the dock, six hundred sounds like a lot, but next to forty thousand it is barely one and a half percent. The word "roughly" keeps it from sounding like a lawyer's defense. She is a person who counted, not someone building a case. Then she puts the word everyone hated hearing at the end of a sentence, after a colon: "the one word nobody wants to hear... wait." Because the word stands alone, the audience hears it again the way they heard it on the dock, only now they hear it from the captain's side.

What keeps this from being self-defense is that Marrow names the cost before anyone else can. "It costs the nurse her shift at the county hospital, the farmer his place in line at the grain scale, the boy his first day of school." These are not abstract inconveniences. They are probably people in the crowd. Listing them shows she was paying attention to who stood on the dock, which is the same kind of attention she says waiting requires. The Dell Ambrose story pushes this to the extreme: a man whose wife is in labor, the most sympathetic argument there is for going. Her answer is four words, "I kept it tied," with no explanation, which is how a decision on the dock actually feels. Then she says she does not tell the story "to make myself the hero of it." There is a tension here, since she was obviously right and the story makes her look good. But by turning down the hero role she makes the story about judgment instead of about herself. She also admits "those forty minutes were the longest stretch of my life," so the audience sees that waiting hurt her too, which makes it hard to call it timid.

Her strongest move is the concession in paragraph five. She grants that "patience can be a disguise for timidity" and even that "somebody lost a day they did not need to lose." This only works because of the credibility she built earlier with the numbers. A captain who refused all the time could not afford to admit she was overcautious. Marrow can, and then she flips it: only the captain who leaves too early has "to stand up in a church and explain herself." The understatement of "I never had to host one here" lets the audience fill in the funerals that never happened. The grumbling town is suddenly the town that never lost anyone.

The tone shifts at the end, from the stern voice of "it does not negotiate" to something almost affectionate. "You forgave me, mostly" is funny, and the "mostly" admits the grumbling was real without holding it against them. This matters because she is also talking to her successor, and to how the town will treat that person. When she says "silence is sometimes the sound of somebody taking care of you," she gives residents a new way to hear the missing horn at seven, and they will need it for a captain who hasn't earned thirty-one years of trust yet. Her last line, thanking them for "the ones we did not make," puts the refusals inside the shared record of crossings. The word "we" is the point. The waiting was something the town did together with her, and she is asking them to keep doing it after she's gone.

In her speech at Landing Day, Ines Marrow uses many rhetorical strategies to show the town that waiting is important and that patience is a good thing. She uses stories, numbers, and a friendly tone to get her point across to the people of Birch Landing.

First, Marrow uses numbers. She says she made about forty thousand crossings and refused about six hundred. This shows that she did not refuse very often, so she was mostly going. This is logos because it uses facts and numbers. It makes the audience see that she was not lazy or scared.

Next, she tells a story about Dell Ambrose and his wife who was having a baby. He told her he would never forgive her if she kept the boat tied. She kept it tied and then forty minutes later the fog lifted and the baby was born fine. This is pathos because it makes the audience feel emotional about the baby. It makes the audience trust her because it shows waiting worked out in the end.

Marrow also talks about the river. She says the river does not negotiate and keeps its own hours. This is personification. It shows that the river is the one in charge and not her, so the town should not blame her for the delays.

At the end she thanks the town for the crossings, including the ones they did not make. She says you forgave me, mostly. This is a nice way to end because it is a goodbye and she is being kind to the audience. It makes them feel good about her and about the next captain.

In conclusion, Marrow uses logos, pathos and ethos to convince the town that patience is care. Her speech works because she uses a lot of different strategies and the audience will probably agree with her by the end.

When Pell Hollow traded worksheets for a creek trail, the parents who worried about polynomials were asking the right question about the wrong subject. Ines Varlow is right that homework is "practice" and a community project is "experience," but she writes as if the two are competing for the same hour of a student's night. They aren't, at least not always. Schools should replace traditional homework with long-term projects only where the homework was never building fluency in the first place, and they should keep the nightly practice that skills like algebra or a foreign language actually need. Even then, the replacement only works if the project is designed for the students who have the least free time, not the most.

Some homework really is the "small, repetitive, private labor" Varlow describes. Last fall in Algebra II I spent most of a week doing thirty logarithm problems a night, and I hated it. But by the Thursday quiz I could rewrite log base 2 of 32 without thinking, and that only happened because I had gotten the same kind of problem wrong maybe fifteen times, alone at my kitchen table. No footbridge campaign would have given me that. A project might use math, like measuring a trail's slope or budgeting lumber, but it uses math a student already has. It doesn't drill it. If a district cut this kind of homework for a project, it would be giving up the one thing the project itself depends on.

A lot of homework, though, isn't practice at all. In my U.S. History class we answered ten comprehension questions for every textbook section, and most people copied the answers from the bold words in the chapter. The assignment measured completion, not thinking. Compare that to what my cousin did at her school in Marlow County. Her class spent a semester recording interviews with people who worked at the old shoe factory before it closed, and then they built a display for the public library. She had to figure out which questions got a nervous seventy-year-old man to open up, check his dates against newspaper archives, and decide what to cut. That is the skill history homework says it teaches, evaluating sources and building an argument from them, except she actually did it. Here the project doesn't replace practice; it replaces a fake version of practice with the real thing. So the line for replacement isn't between subjects like "math" and "history." It's between assignments that build a skill and assignments that only prove time was spent.

The strongest objection to projects is not that they are messy, which Varlow already admits, but that they are unequal. Freshman year our biology class did a water-testing project at Grant Pond that was supposed to replace a month of lab worksheets. Within two weeks it was obvious which groups had a parent who could drive them to the pond on Saturdays and which had members working shifts at the grocery store. The kids with jobs ended up making the poster while everyone else did the science, and the grades showed it. A worksheet, for all its boredom, can be done at 11 p.m. after a shift. If schools replace homework with projects, they have to put the project hours inside the school day or provide rides, or else "experience" turns into something only students with free afternoons can afford.

That is also my answer to Varlow's last question about who sets the ratio. The people who grade the work know which assignments are busywork, but the people who "live with the results" include students whose evenings are already full. A school should decide subject by subject, and really assignment by assignment, with both groups in the room. The creek trail may be worth forty hours. Just not the forty hours a kid needed to learn to factor a polynomial, and not forty hours that only part of the class could show up for.
